source.title: Unlearn to Relearn Backdoors: Deferred Backdoor Functionality Attacks on Deep Learning Models

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a concealed, unlearned backdoor in vision models can reactivate during benign fine-tuning, extending the recovery question to a different domain and an attacker-designed method.
record.gate_note: This is a deferred-backdoor attack study, not a study of LLM factual-knowledge unlearning. Its fine-tuning experiments bear on recovery after concealment. The detection-method scores and output-distribution analyses are not rows for the claim versions unless they measure the stated recovery or mechanism.
record.test_reason: The study is a vision backdoor attack paper. The attacker deliberately builds a fragile, partial-layer 'unlearning' of a planted trigger (DeferBad) so that benign fine-tuning reactivates it. It then reports its own attack's success (ASR) and stealth. It does not measure whether ordinary unlearning methods on LLMs remove targeted knowledge. The reversibility is induced on purpose, and the systems are CNN classifiers (ResNet18, VGG16, EfficientNet-B0), not LLMs. It borrows the 'suppressed behaviour re-emerges on retraining' insight (citing Qi et al. 2023) as a design tool. So it uses the finding without testing it; its rows bear on no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors present DeferBad as an attack that conceals a planted vision backdoor (near-zero ASR) and has it reactivate under routine benign fine-tuning, while evading most detectors. Effectiveness varies by dataset, architecture and trigger. They call for lifecycle-long security checks and note that the work is limited to vision tasks.
record.recipe_differences: DeferBad deliberately injects a vision backdoor, partially updates selected layers with an unlearning dataset to conceal it, then uses benign fine-tuning to reactivate it; it is not an LLM knowledge-unlearning recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery varies with model architecture, attack type, dataset, corruption severity, and fine-tuning strategy or number of updated layers. The authors report occasional ASR below 10% when more layers are fine-tuned, and a Tiny ImageNet EfficientNet-B0 BadNet result changes from 0.04% to near 30% when fine-tuning all layers (k = 0).

fits_no_version.finding: A backdoor deliberately concealed by partial-layer unlearning in vision CNNs (ASR ~0-1%) is reactivated by benign fine-tuning. Reactivation reaches up to ~98% ASR on CIFAR-10/CIFAR10-C, but is weak or absent in some Tiny ImageNet settings (e.g., VGG16 BadNet on Tiny ImageNet-C: 0%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attacker-engineered, deliberately fragile unlearning of a backdoor in vision models can be reversed by benign fine-tuning, with strength depending on architecture, trigger and dataset.

record.problems: The experiments are limited to vision models and intentionally engineered backdoors, so they do not establish the same effect for LLM factual knowledge or ordinary unlearning methods. No uncertainty estimates are stated. The mechanism is mainly a qualitative explanation, and the authors say further theoretical investigation is needed. Table 3's prose and table disagree on EfficientNet-B0 ISSBA CIFAR-10 after-fine-tuning ASR (61.68% versus 58.17%).
record.rows_left_out: Due to the 60-row limit, omitted individual fine-tuning results from Appendix Tables 6 and 7 outside the reported Tiny ImageNet-C VGG16 BadNet failures, as well as additional settings in Figures 2 and 4. These include other CIFAR10-C corruption types and Tiny ImageNet-C results; the paper's prose summarizes several but does not provide a complete numerical transcription in the main discussion.

untested.parts: No standard unlearning method, LLM, targeted-knowledge accuracy, or simple attack on naturally unlearned models.
No relearning attack on LLM unlearning; fine-tuning only reactivates a deliberately fragile vision backdoor concealment.
No activation-direction ablation or internal analysis of an unlearning method.
Quantization mentioned only as future work.
No robust unlearning method proposed or tested.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' with labels on A, B and C is overturned. This is a security attack in which reversibility is engineered by the attacker, in vision classifiers. It is not evidence about whether genuine LLM unlearning is shallow. At most it is a loose analogy, recorded under fits_no_version. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test current LLM unlearning methods, their targeted knowledge accuracy, or simple recovery attacks on naturally unlearned models.

Fine-tuning uses clean vision data (including held-out data or corrupted-data settings), not unrelated LLM examples or a subset of forgotten facts. The paper does not establish the effect of a few examples in an LLM.
No activation-direction ablation is performed. The proposed blocking-versus-deletion mechanism is discussed qualitatively, not isolated by a direct internal causal test.
Quantization is mentioned as future work only.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language, or in-context recovery experiments.
Does not test a robust counter-method to the listed LLM unlearning attacks.

rows.subject: DeferBad
rows.operation_detail: Authors' qualitative account of concealment and reactivation mechanism
rows.measure: Whether concealment deletes backdoor features or suppresses their expression
rows.value: The paper says updated layers counteract backdoor behavior in other layers and that subsequent fine-tuning disrupts this suppression; it describes latent backdoor information as remaining in other layers.
rows.locator: Appendix C, Discussion on Concealment Mechanism
rows.note: The authors say the exact mathematical mechanism needs further theoretical investigation; this is a proposed explanation, not a direct ablation or causal test.
rows.check: Not a result row. It is the authors' qualitative account of their own engineered concealment, with no internal ablation or causal test. It concerns an attack design, not whether LLM unlearning methods block rather than delete.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
